questions.prompt: After Chapter 16 defines strategic rigor, what does Chapter 17 add?
choices: The thinking habits needed to practice that rigor well
A rejection of diagnosis and judgment
A claim that strategy is mostly optimism
questions.explanation: Chapter 17 turns from rigorous standards to the mindset that keeps those standards alive in practice.

questions.prompt: What does using your head mean in this chapter?
choices: Being naturally clever without discipline
Active judgment that questions easy stories and weak analogies
Trusting the first coherent explanation
questions.explanation: The chapter uses the title to mean disciplined thought, not abstract intelligence or fast confidence.

questions.prompt: Which strategic risk does the chapter warn about most clearly?
choices: Testing whether a comparison fits
Letting familiarity or wishful interpretation substitute for diagnosis
Revising a story when evidence changes
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that mental shortcuts can corrupt strategy before the plan is even built.

questions.prompt: A class proposal relies on a clean comparison, but no one checks whether the comparison truly fits the problem. What is the Chapter 17 diagnosis?
choices: The proposal is stronger because the analogy is memorable
The group is letting analogy replace disciplined judgment
The proposal only needs more confidence
questions.explanation: Chapter 17 treats analogy as useful only when it is tested rather than trusted automatically.

choices: Because it keeps the strategist from accepting the first comfortable interpretation as if it were insight
Because skepticism means rejecting all action
Because skepticism removes uncertainty
questions.explanation: The chapter defines skepticism as active judgment, not cynicism or paralysis.

choices: By showing what kind of mind can sustain rigorous strategy under real conditions
By replacing rigor with personality
By treating strategy as separate from judgment
questions.explanation: Chapter 16 defines rigorous standards; Chapter 17 shows that those standards depend on disciplined thinking habits.

questions.prompt: A personal decision improves after someone questions the story they want to believe. What chapter idea is this showing?
choices: Disciplined thought resisting wishful interpretation
Proof that strategy is irrelevant in personal life
Evidence that confidence is enough without diagnosis
questions.explanation: The example shows better judgment emerging when preference stops controlling the reading of reality.

questions.prompt: What is the best sign that a strategist is thinking on autopilot?
choices: They keep testing fit before acting
They accept a familiar story because it feels coherent and comfortable
They revise a comparison when evidence disagrees
questions.explanation: Autopilot thinking accepts coherence and familiarity too quickly instead of examining them.

questions.prompt: Why do better thinking habits improve judgment without removing uncertainty?
choices: Because disciplined thought helps the strategist read reality better even when the fog remains
Because disciplined thought guarantees control
Because uncertainty disappears when analogies are clear
questions.explanation: The chapter rejects fake certainty. Better thinking strengthens judgment inside uncertainty.

questions.prompt: How does the book finally close in Chapter 17?
choices: By arguing that strategy ultimately depends on the quality of thought the strategist brings to reality
By abandoning the earlier concepts
By saying method no longer matters
questions.explanation: The final chapter lands on strategist mindset: the book's strategic ideas depend on disciplined thought applying them.
